parts.label: Part 4
parts.article:
Today, I’m going to talk about the history and technological development of coal mining on Cape Breton Island, located off the east coast of Canada in Nova Scotia. This area played a critical role in Canada’s energy production for over two centuries. Let’s begin with the early days. Coal mining in Cape Breton dates back to the 1720s during the French colonial period. These first operations were extremely basic. The miners didn’t use machines. They relied on manual labour to gather the coal. In fact, the earliest coal was moved by hand from the base of the cliffs along the island’s coast. It was a harsh and dangerous task, as workers had to navigate slippery rocks while carrying heavy loads of coal in baskets. Now, as demand for coal increased, it became clear that new systems had to be developed to handle the growing volume. The ability to transport coal efficiently became one of the biggest challenges facing the industry. For production to grow, Cape Breton needed a well-organised transport network. Initially, they used horse-drawn carts, but as output rose, they introduced railway lines that could carry larger quantities to the port for shipping. This increase in industrial activity also brought about changes in the workforce. Every year, particularly in spring, new groups of labourers would arrive to take advantage of seasonal jobs. Spring was an ideal time, not just because of the weather, but because mining operations expanded significantly during the warmer months. By summer, mines would be fully staffed with both local residents and new arrivals from other parts of Canada and abroad. Naturally, this shift in employment patterns had consequences for local demographics. Many people who had lived in remote or agricultural areas began to relocate. Villages near the mines grew, while the population in more rural regions started to decline. Families often moved together, and mining towns quickly expanded, sometimes without adequate planning or infrastructure. By the early 20th century, Cape Breton had become a major player in the national coal industry. At its peak, the island was supplying around 40% of all coal used in Canada. This boom not only supported the domestic energy supply, but also provided fuel for export to other countries.

Let’s talk about the workers themselves. Around the year 1800, the local workforce could no longer meet the demand. To fill the gap, labourers were recruited from abroad. Most of the early migrants came from Scotland, particularly from mining towns in the central and western regions. These skilled Scottish miners brought valuable knowledge and traditions with them, shaping the way mining was carried out in Canada. Italian workers also played a key role, especially in the construction of railways and tunnels.

Now, let's look at the technology used in underground mining, specifically how the tunnels were lit before electricity became widespread.

The earliest source of light was a grease torch. This simple tool burned animal fat to produce a flickering flame. It was cheap and easy to make, but produced a lot of smoke and posed a serious fire risk.

A slightly improved version was to mount a candle in a metal or clay holder. These holders were usually attached to the timber supports inside the tunnels. While candles were more manageable than grease torches, they still had open flames and were far from safe in gas-prone environments.

The invention of the Davy lamp marked a huge step forward in mine safety. This device had a flame enclosed in mesh and featured a fitted link sealed by a lock. The design controlled the airflow and prevented the flame from igniting any methane gas in the air. Because of this innovation, the number of accidents, such as explosions or fires, dropped significantly across many mining sites.

Later, carbide lamps were introduced. These worked by combining calcium carbide with water, which created acetylene gas. When lit, it gave off a steady yellow-white flame that was much brighter than previous sources. These lamps were widely used until electric lighting eventually replaced them in the 20th century.

In fact, the earliest coal was moved by hand from the base of the cliffs along the island’s coast.
不要填 coast（海岸），虽然录音提到了 coast，但具体的取煤地点是 base of the cliffs（悬崖底部），且 coast 在修饰 cliffs。
For production to grow, Cape Breton needed a well-organised transport network.
不要填 railway（铁路），录音中铁路是后来作为例子引入的，用来解决运输问题的具体手段。
录音说为了增加产量，布雷顿角需要一个组织良好的 transport（运输）网络，对应题干 development of the ... system（system 和 network 是同义替换）。
Every year, particularly in spring, new groups of labourers would arrive to take advantage of seasonal jobs.
你可能想填 abroad（国外），但录音说的是 laborers would arrive 在春天，如果是填地点，通常会说 from other parts，而这里强调的是季节性的劳工流动。
录音提到每年 spring（春天）都会有新的一批劳工到达，对应题干 every year from...（这里的 from 表示时间起点，即“从春天开始”）。
Villages near the mines grew, while the population in more rural regions started to decline.
不要填 remote（偏远），虽然录音提到了 remote or agricultural areas，但紧接着明确说是 population in more rural regions started to decline。
录音中说随着矿区发展，rural（农村）地区的人口开始下降，对应题干 population was reduced in ... areas。
At its peak, the island was supplying around 40% of all coal used in Canada.
听到数字要敏感，直接抓取 40% 即可，不需要进行复杂的换算。
听到 At its peak（在顶峰时期）定位，录音明确说该岛供应了大约 40% 的加拿大用煤。
录音提到大约1800年时，大部分早期移民来自 Scotland（苏格兰），对应题干 most miners were from...。
Most of the early migrants came from Scotland, particularly from mining towns in the central and western regions.
注意不要填 Italy，那是后来才提到的参与铁路建设的工人，不是 Around 1800 这个时间点的。
